newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Congo canoe exodus quits Brazzaville for Kinshasa.
newsitem.headline: Congo canoe exodus quits Brazzaville for Kinshasa.

text.p: Hundreds of residents of Brazzaville braved strong currents and a closed river frontier on Sunday to flee bloody street fighting in the Congolese capital by paddling their canoes to neighbouring Kinshasa.
The mighty Congo river which separates Brazzaville and the capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo was dotted with the canoes loaded mostly with men, but also some women and children.

Many of those escaping fighting between a political militia loyal to ex-president Denis Sassou Nguesso and troops loyal to President Pascal Lissouba, had come from Kinshasa to seek work in Brazzaville.
Others had left Kinshasa for fear of looting when Laurent Kabila's troops advanced on the capital of the former Zaire last month, ousting President Mobutu Sese Seko,and renaming the country.

"They are killing people all over the city," said Cleophas Kabeya, a young man who sold key rings and immitation Swiss watches on the streets of Brazzaville to make a living. "I don't want to go back ever".
Kabeya said he had left his stock with a friend in Brazzaville and had no money to take a taxi the 25 km (16 miles) to his family's home in Ndjili, a squalid suburb of the city of five million.
He said that he braved an eruption of fighting between Brazzaville militias in 1993 in which at least 2,000 people died, but this time the fighting was more widespread.
In theory the river frontier between the twin capitals has been officially closed since Kabila's army marched into Kinshasa -- provoking the last exodus across the river.

In practice oarsmen have continued to brave the strong currents and the rules of Kabila's new order to make the thirty minute journey across an old 1.6 km (one mile) smuggling route, used for years to traffic goods from one city to the other.
On arrival in Kinshasa the travellers are frisked, and their mostly meagre possesions searched. But Kabila's soldiers allow them to pass peacefully.
Escapees from Brazzaville said crossing the city to get to the river bank had been the most difficult part of their ordeal.

"I walked all the way from the city centre and there were bodies all over the streets, by dozens and dozens," said one woman trader, who had brought her wheelbarrow full of plastic buckets through Brazzaville and across the river.
